The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review of Clinical Evidence, Current Challenges, and Future Perspectives

### Introduction and Development
For decades, the transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (TV-ICD) has been the gold standard for preventing sudden cardiac death (SCD). However, TV-ICD systems are associated with notable short- and long-term complications, primarily related to lead placement within the cardiovascular system, such as systemic bacteremia, endocarditis, venous occlusion, and lead fracture. To address these vulnerabilities, the subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed, offering an entirely extravascular approach to defibrillation [1]. Since its regulatory approval, clinical studies have evaluated its performance, demonstrating rapid adoption and robust clinical efficacy across various patient populations [2,3].

### Surgical Technique and Implantation Considerations
The S-ICD system consists of a subcutaneous pulse generator positioned near the left midaxillary line (between the serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi muscles) and a subcutaneous lead positioned parasternally. This configuration completely avoids the cardiovascular system, preserving venous access and protecting the heart from direct lead-related mechanical damage. Initially, a three-incision technique (requiring a pocket incision, a xiphoid incision, and a superior parasternal incision) was the standard approach [4]. Over time, clinical experience led to the development of a simplified two-incision technique that omits the superior parasternal incision [5]. This modification reduces surgical times, decreases the potential for device-associated discomfort, and yields better cosmetic outcomes. While early implantations relied on general anesthesia, modern practices increasingly utilize regional anesthetic techniques, such as serratus anterior plane blocks, combined with deep sedation or local anesthesia, to ensure patient comfort and optimize procedural efficiency [6].

### Clinical Trials and Real-World Registries
The clinical profile of the S-ICD has been thoroughly characterized through rigorous clinical registries and randomized trials. Early pooled analyses of the Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) trial and the EFFORTLESS registry confirmed that the S-ICD safely terminates induced and spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias with high efficacy [7]. Medium- to long-term follow-up from the EFFORTLESS registry demonstrated that these outcomes remain stable over time, with low rates of systemic infection and device-related complications [8]. Systematic reviews of procedural data also identified a clear learning curve, showing that complication rates, pocket hematomas, and skin erosion decreased significantly as operators gained experience [9,10].

The landmark PRAETORIAN trial provided the first randomized, head-to-head comparison between the S-ICD and TV-ICD systems [11]. The trial demonstrated that the S-ICD was non-inferior to the TV-ICD with respect to the composite primary endpoint of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks. To evaluate whether optimal programming could further lower inappropriate shock rates, the UNTOUCHED trial enrolled primary prevention patients with low ejection fractions. This study showed extremely low rates of inappropriate shocks, highlighting the effectiveness of dual-zone programming and advanced filtering [12]. Real-world registries across diverse populations, including the US Post-Approval Study and European cohorts, have replicated these positive findings [13,14]. Notably, because of the complete absence of intravascular hardware, the S-ICD has emerged as an especially valuable alternative for patients at extremely high risk for systemic or lead-related infections, such as patients with end-stage renal disease undergoing chronic hemodialysis [15].

### Patient Selection and Screening
Unlike traditional transvenous systems that detect near-field intracardiac electrograms, the S-ICD utilizes far-field subcutaneous signals that resemble a surface ECG. This makes S-ICD systems susceptible to sensing physiological signals other than the QRS complex, most notably T-wave oversensing (TWO), which can lead to inappropriate shocks [16]. Consequently, pre-implantation ECG screening is mandatory to evaluate the patient's QRS-to-T-wave ratio. While screening was initially performed manually using paper templates across three vectors in both supine and standing positions [17], automated screening tools have since been integrated into clinical practice. These tools reduce manual reading errors and offer highly reproducible results [18]. To further mitigate TWO, advanced signal processing features, such as the SMART Pass software filter, have been developed and deployed [19]. Comparative clinical studies demonstrate that these sophisticated algorithms allow S-ICD systems to achieve arrhythmia discrimination profiles comparable to those of TV-ICDs [20], resulting in a substantial reduction in inappropriate therapy rates in real-world settings [21].

### Limitations and Special Populations
Despite its compelling advantages, S-ICD therapy has specific clinical limitations. Because it lacks direct contact with the myocardium, the device cannot deliver long-term bradycardia pacing or anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP) to terminate monomorphic ventricular tachycardia [22]. While newer-generation S-ICD systems feature enhanced battery longevity and improved software algorithms to optimize performance [23], complications such as pocket infections and lead migration can still occur [24]. Nonetheless, the S-ICD has become a preferred therapy for specific patient groups, including young individuals with channelopathies such as Brugada syndrome [25] or patients with complex congenital heart disease who lack venous access to the right ventricle [26]. Procedural protocols continue to evolve; for example, although early protocols mandated intraoperative defibrillation testing (DFT), modern data suggest that DFT may be safely bypassed in selected low-risk patients undergoing implantation, reducing procedural complexity and anesthetic requirements [27].

### Future Directions: Modular Therapy
To address the lack of pacing capabilities, the concept of modular cardiac rhythm management has emerged. This paradigm pairs the S-ICD with a leadless pacemaker (LP) implanted directly into the right ventricle [28]. Preclinical and early clinical feasibility studies have demonstrated that these two independent devices can communicate effectively via wireless intrabody signaling [29]. This integrated system allows the LP to deliver bradycardia pacing and ATP when triggered by the S-ICD, while the S-ICD retains its capacity to deliver high-energy shocks if pacing fails. Ongoing trials continue to evaluate the safety and clinical efficacy of these modular, fully extravascular systems, which promise to combine the benefits of both technologies [30].
